items.title: Rufus Reid interviewed by Monk Rowe, Atlanta, GA, January 4, 2013
items.q: [INTERVIEWER] I think it was Marian McPartland who said, via Alec Wilder, “I’d kill for a good bass line.”

ctx.x: No. Montgomery, Alabama. I joined the — I was in the Air Force. I was going to get drafted, and someone says well if you pass the audition for the Air Force Band, you’ll automatically get in the band if you pass, but in the Air Force there’s no guarantees that I was going to get a chance — it was either trumpet or rifle or something. So none of that. But I taught myself those things. But no one told me about how important piano was, like the kids today now. And it was a revelation of learning the harmony. I mean…

I always think that the bass player has the most challenging job in the band. I mean I love the bass. And I think it was Marian McPartland who said, via Alec Wilder, “I’d kill for a good bass line.” Something like that. But I’ve often wondered, what do you do, I read about you playing in Chicago with these fellas who would come through. And they call a tune and you don’t know it. And usually the piano player is following the bass player. But if you don’t know it, what do you do in that situation?

Well I mean generally the pianists are the ones that — we hope one of us knows the song. But I learned when the piano players knew it and they would — a really good pianist, particularly coming from that ilk of players, the Jimmy Rowles, the Hank Jones, the Tommy Flanagans, they could lead me, if I could see their hands, they could lead me by watching. I also learned the piano a little bit more because now I started really watching so I knew the names of the notes really well. But then they would just lead me.…
